PRE-INTERMEDIATE 1Unit 1 · Lesson 1
Story · Lesson 1

The New Student

A new level, a new student. Read the story, answer the questions, then read it again from Omar's point of view.

Say who people areSay where people are fromSay how people feel

1The story

Today is the first day of a new level. Adam and Sara are in the class. They are happy.

There is a new student. His name is Omar. He is from Port Sudan. He isn't from Khartoum. Port Sudan is a city on the Red Sea. It is hot, but it is beautiful.

Omar is nineteen. He is friendly, but he is a little nervous. It is his first day, and the students aren't his friends yet.

Mr. Ali is the teacher. He is kind and funny. "Welcome to the class, Omar!" Adam and Sara are friendly, too. Now Omar isn't nervous. He is happy.

2Questions and answers Answer fast. Short answers are fine.

1
Is it the first day of a new level?Yes, it is.
2
Are Adam and Sara in the class?Yes, they are.
3
Who is the new student?Omar.
4
Is Omar from Khartoum?No, he isn't. He's from Port Sudan.
5
Where is Port Sudan?On the Red Sea.
6
Is Port Sudan cold or hot?Hot. It's hot, but it's beautiful.
7
How old is Omar?He's nineteen.
8
Is Omar nervous?Yes, he is. It's his first day.
9
Are the students his friends?No, they aren't. Not yet.
10
Who is the teacher?Mr. Ali.
11
Is Mr. Ali kind?Yes, he is. He's kind and funny.
12
Is Omar nervous now?No, he isn't. He's happy.

3Point of view Now Omar tells the story.

O

Today is the first day of a new level. I am a new student. My name is Omar. I'm from Port Sudan. I'm not from Khartoum. Port Sudan is a city on the Red Sea. It is hot, but it is beautiful.

I'm nineteen. I'm friendly, but I'm a little nervous. The students aren't my friends yet.

Mr. Ali is our teacher. He is kind and funny. Adam and Sara are friendly, too. Now I'm not nervous. I'm happy.

4What did you learn?

You learned the verb be.

We use it to say who people are, where they are from, and how they feel.

Ihe · she · ityou · we · they
amisare
I'mhe'sthey're
I'm nothe isn'tthey aren't
Am I …?Is he …?Are you …?
Short forms: 'm · 's · 'reWe usually speak with short forms: I'm, he's, they're.
Not: isn't · aren'tHe isn't from Khartoum. They aren't his friends.
Questions: be comes firstHe is nineteen. → Is he nineteen?
QuestionsIs he from Khartoum?Yes, he is. / No, he isn't.

5New words

citya big town
beautifulvery nice to look at
friendlykind and nice to other people
nervousa little afraid of something new
yetuntil now

Topic · Lesson 2

Places in My City

The places we go every day, and where they are.

Name places in a citySay where a place is

1Read

This is Khartoum. It is Adam's city. It is big and busy, and there are many places in it.

The market is in the city center. It is open every day, and it is always busy. The bus station is near the market. There are buses to every part of the city.

There is a small café near the institute. The tea there is very good. The bank is next to the hospital. The hospital is big and clean.

And where is the institute? It is on a quiet street, near the café.

4

Conversation · Lesson 3

Where Are You?

On the phone, asking and saying where you are

Start and end a callAsk where someone isSay where a place is

1Read the conversation

After class, Omar is in the city center. He calls Adam on the phone.
OOMARHello, Adam? It's Omar.
AADAMHi, Omar! Where are you?
OOMARI'm in the city center. I'm at the market.
AADAMOh, I'm near the market, too. I'm at the bus station.
OOMARGreat! Is there a café near you?
AADAMYes, there is. It's next to the bank.
OOMARIs it a big café?
AADAMNo, it isn't. It's small, but the tea is very good.
OOMARPerfect. See you there in ten minutes!
AADAMSee you!

2Useful phrases

Start a call

Hello, Adam? It's Omar.
— Hi, Omar!

Ask where

Where are you?
— I'm at the market.

Ask about a place

Is there a café near you?
— Yes, there is.

Say where it is

It's next to the bank.
It's near the market.

Make a plan

See you there in ten minutes!

End a call

See you! · Bye!

3New words

calltalk to someone on the phone
perfectvery good; just right
minutesa minute is sixty seconds
therein that place

Story · Lesson 4

Adam's Day

A short story about a normal day. Read it, answer the questions, then read it again from Adam's point of view.

Talk about your dayAnswer quick questionsTell a story about you
6:00wakes up
8:00English class
1:00lunch at home
Eveninghomework, football
10:00bed

1The story

Adam lives in Khartoum. He is a student at Future Vision Institute.

Every day, Adam wakes up at six o'clock. He drinks tea with milk, and he eats bread and beans. Then he takes the bus to the institute.

His English class starts at eight. Adam likes his class. He reads, he listens, and he speaks a lot. Mr. Ali is his teacher.

At one o'clock, Adam goes home. He has lunch with his family. In the evening, he does his homework and watches football on TV. He goes to bed at ten.

2Questions and answers Answer fast. Short answers are fine.

1
Where does Adam live?In Khartoum.
2
Is Adam a teacher?No, he isn't. He's a student.
3
Does Adam wake up at six?Yes, he does.
4
Does he wake up at nine?No, he doesn't. He wakes up at six.
5
Does he drink coffee or tea?Tea. He drinks tea with milk.
6
What does he eat?Bread and beans.
7
How does he go to the institute?He takes the bus.
8
When does his class start?At eight.
9
Does Adam like his class?Yes, he does. He likes it a lot.
10
Who is his teacher?Mr. Ali.
11
What does he watch on TV?Football. He watches football.
12
When does he go to bed?At ten.

3Point of view Now Adam tells the story.

A

Every day, I wake up at six o'clock. I drink tea with milk, and I eat bread and beans. Then I take the bus to the institute.

My English class starts at eight. I like my class. I read, I listen, and I speak a lot. Mr. Ali is my teacher.

At one o'clock, I go home. I have lunch with my family. In the evening, I do my homework and watch football on TV. I go to bed at ten.

Topic · Lesson 5

Time and Days

The days of the week, the weekend in Sudan, and how to say the time.

Say the days of the weekSay the timeTalk about your week

1Read

There are seven days in a week. In Sudan, the weekend is Friday and Saturday. Most people work and study from Sunday to Thursday.

Adam goes to the institute five days a week. His class starts at eight o'clock and ends at one o'clock. On Friday, he stays at home with his family.

How do we say the time? We say the hour first, then the minutes. 8:00 is eight o'clock, and 8:30 is eight thirty.

Story · Lesson 7

Sara Doesn't Like Fish

Every Friday, Sara's family eats fish. Sara doesn't. Read the story, then read it again from Sara's point of view.

Say what you like and don't likeAsk with Do and DoesAnswer Yes I do and No I don't

1The story

Sara lives with her family. Every Friday, her mother cooks fish for lunch. Her father likes fish. Her little sister, Lina, likes fish, too. But Sara doesn't like fish. She doesn't eat it.

"Do you want some fish, Sara?" her mother asks. "No, thank you," Sara says. "I don't like fish." So Sara eats rice and salad.

One Friday, her mother doesn't cook fish. She cooks chicken. Sara is happy. But her father doesn't eat much, and Lina doesn't smile. They don't like Friday without fish!

The next Friday, Sara cooks lunch. She makes fish with lemon and rice. Her family loves it. And Sara? She eats a little fish, and she likes it!

2Questions and answers Answer fast. Short answers are fine.

1
Does Sara's mother cook fish every Friday?Yes, she does.
2
Does Sara's father like fish?Yes, he does.
3
Does Lina like fish?Yes, she does.
4
Does Sara like fish?No, she doesn't.
5
Does Sara eat fish or rice?Rice. She eats rice and salad.
6
What does Sara say to her mother?"No, thank you. I don't like fish."
7
What does her mother cook one Friday?Chicken.
8
Is Sara happy?Yes, she is.
9
Does Lina smile?No, she doesn't.
10
Who cooks lunch the next Friday?Sara.
11
What does she make?Fish with lemon and rice.
12
Does Sara like the fish?Yes, she does!

3Point of view Now Sara tells the story.

S

I live with my family. Every Friday, my mother cooks fish for lunch. My father likes fish, and my little sister, Lina, likes fish, too. But I don't like fish. I don't eat it.

"Do you want some fish, Sara?" my mother asks. "No, thank you. I don't like fish." So I eat rice and salad.

One Friday, my mother doesn't cook fish. She cooks chicken. I'm happy. But my father doesn't eat much, and Lina doesn't smile. They don't like Friday without fish!

The next Friday, I cook lunch. I make fish with lemon and rice. My family loves it. And me? I eat a little fish, and I like it!

4What did you learn?

You learned don't and doesn't.

We use them to say no in the present simple. To ask, we start with Do or Does.

I · you · we · theyhe · she · it
I like fish.She likes fish.
I don't like fish.She doesn't like fish.
Do you like fish?Does she like fish?
Yes, I do. / No, I don't.Yes, she does. / No, she doesn't.
don't = do notWe usually say don't and doesn't.
After doesn't: no -sShe doesn't like fish. Not: doesn't likes.
Questions start with Do / DoesDo you want some fish? Does Lina like fish?
QuestionsDoes Sara like fish?Yes, she does. / No, she doesn't.

Topic · Lesson 8

Meals in Sudan

When we eat, what we eat, and the things in the kitchen.

Talk about mealsName things in the kitchenSay what people like

1Read

In Sudan, people eat three meals a day. Breakfast is often late, at about ten o'clock. Many people eat beans with bread, oil, and cheese.

Lunch is the big meal of the day. People eat it at home, at about three or four o'clock, after work and school. Dinner is small and late. Some people only drink tea with milk.

Do Sudanese people like sweet tea? Yes, they do! Many people don't drink tea without sugar.

In the kitchen, we cook rice in a pot and eggs in a pan. We put food on a plate, and we eat with a spoon or with bread.

2Three meals

breakfastabout 10:00 · beans and bread
lunchabout 3:00 · the big meal
dinnerlate · a small meal

3In the kitchen

potfor rice and soup
panfor eggs
platewe put food on it
spoonfor rice and soup
forkfor salad and meat
cupfor tea and coffee

4Questions and answers Answer fast. Short answers are fine.

1
How many meals do people eat in Sudan?Three: breakfast, lunch, and dinner.
2
When is breakfast?At about ten o'clock.
3
What do many people eat for breakfast?Beans with bread, oil, and cheese.
4
What is the big meal of the day?Lunch.
5
Do people eat a big dinner?No, they don't. Dinner is small.
6

5New words

Story · Lesson 10

Omar Can't Cook

Omar can do many things, but not one important thing. Read the story, then read it again from Omar's point of view.

Say what you can doSay what you can't doAsk with Can you

1The story

Omar lives in a small apartment near the institute. His family is in Port Sudan. Omar can do many things. He can play football very well. He can speak Arabic and English. He can fix phones, too.

But Omar can't cook. He can make tea, but he can't make lunch. Every day, he eats sandwiches. He is tired of sandwiches!

One evening, he calls his mother. "Can you help me, Mom? I can't cook!" His mother laughs. "Of course I can. Take a pot, some rice, water, and salt." Omar listens and writes.

Now Omar can cook rice. He can't cook fish yet, but he can make rice and eggs. He invites Adam for lunch. "Your rice is good!" Adam says. Omar smiles. "Next week: fish!"

2Questions and answers Answer fast. Short answers are fine.

1
Where does Omar live?In a small apartment near the institute.
2
Where is his family?In Port Sudan.
3
Can Omar play football?Yes, he can. He can play very well.
4
Can he speak English?Yes, he can. He can speak Arabic and English.
5
Can he fix phones?Yes, he can.
6
Can Omar cook?No, he can't.
7
Can he make tea?Yes, he can.
8
What does he eat every day?Sandwiches.
9
Who does he call?His mother.
10
Can Omar cook rice now?Yes, he can.
11
Can he cook fish?No, he can't. Not yet.
12
Who comes for lunch?Adam.

3Point of view Now Omar tells the story.

O

I live in a small apartment near the institute. My family is in Port Sudan. I can do many things. I can play football very well. I can speak Arabic and English. I can fix phones, too.

But I can't cook. I can make tea, but I can't make lunch. Every day, I eat sandwiches. I'm tired of sandwiches!

One evening, I call my mother. "Can you help me, Mom? I can't cook!" She laughs. "Of course I can." I listen and write.

Now I can cook rice. I can't cook fish yet, but I can make rice and eggs. Adam comes for lunch. "Your rice is good!" he says. "Next week: fish!"

4What did you learn?

You learned can and can't.

We use them to say what we are able to do, and what we are not able to do.

cancan't
I can cook rice.I can't cook fish.
He can play football.He can't cook.
They can speak English.They can't fix cars.
can is the same for everyoneI can, he can, they can. Not: he cans.
After can: the verb onlyHe can cook. Not: can to cook.
can't = cannotWe usually say can't.
QuestionsCan you cook?Yes, I can. / No, I can't.

Topic · Lesson 11

Numbers and Prices

Big numbers, prices, and how we buy things at the market.

Say big numbersAsk the priceAsk How much and How many

1Read

Numbers are everywhere, in prices, phone numbers, and times. We count in tens like this, and then we put two numbers together. We say 25 as twenty-five, and 150 as one hundred fifty.

At the market, prices are in Sudanese pounds. We ask about the price with How much. How much is it? How much are the oranges?

We buy fruit and vegetables by the kilo. For things we can count, like eggs and oranges, we ask How many. How many eggs do you want?

How Much Are the Tomatoes?

Buying food at the market

Ask the priceAsk for an amountAsk for a lower price

1Read the conversation

On Saturday morning, Omar is at the market. He needs tomatoes and eggs for his lunch.
OOMARGood morning. How much are the tomatoes?
SESELLERTwo thousand pounds a kilo.
OOMARCan I have two kilos, please?
SESELLERSure. Anything else?
OOMARTen eggs, please. How much are they?
SESELLERTen eggs are two thousand.
OOMARSo that's six thousand. Can you make it five thousand five hundred?
SESELLERHmm. OK, five thousand five hundred, for a good customer!
OOMARThank you! Here you are.
SESELLERThank you. See you next time!

2Useful phrases

Ask the price

How much are the tomatoes?
— Two thousand a kilo.

Ask for an amount

Can I have two kilos, please?
— Sure.

Count things

Ten eggs, please.

Add it up

So that's six thousand.

Ask for a lower price

Can you make it five thousand five hundred?
— OK!

Say goodbye

See you next time!

3New words

tomatoesred vegetables for salad and cooking
make itchange the price to
customera person who buys from a shop
next timethe time we meet again
